transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. It’s... well, it’s nice to meet you too. I suppose it’s a bit surreal for me to be on this side of the room. I’m a social worker myself—mental health and substance abuse, actually—so I’m usually the one sitting in your chair, asking that exact same opening question and trying to draw people out. 

But... I guess what finally brought me in today is that I feel like the part of me that used to reach for people has just gone very, very quiet. It’s hard to fully articulate, even with my background. I used to take so much genuine pleasure in my work, which is demanding, as you know, but it used to really fill my cup. And my life outside of the clinic, too. I was so dedicated to my yoga practice, I would spend my weekends wandering through different art galleries downtown, I was constantly journaling my thoughts... I had all these vibrant routines that made me feel engaged with the world. 

But lately, it’s like someone just turned the volume down on my entire inner life to zero. Even journaling, which used to be my main way of processing everything, just feels completely empty. I’m mostly just moving through obligations now. I wake up, I check the boxes, I see my clients, I come home, but there's no spark left. There's no desire to actually participate in my own life or connect with anyone. It's just this flat, heavy quietness where my drive used to be, and honestly, it’s starting to become quite distressing to just constantly be going through the motions day in and day out without actually feeling any real connection to what I'm doing...
Have you experienced a period of time like this before in your life, or is this the first time you have felt this way?

You know, I’ve been asking myself that exact same question for weeks now. Because, naturally, given my training, I try to psychoanalyze myself—which is a terrible habit, I know, we make the worst patients. But I’ve really been digging through my own history, trying to find some sort of precedent for this, looking for a pattern. And... no. I really haven't. 

I mean, sure, I’ve had periods of professional burnout. When I was finishing my master's degree in my twenties, for instance, I was working full-time while doing my clinical field placements, and I was just absolutely bone-tired. I’d come home and just collapse on the couch. Or even a few years ago, when our clinic was understaffed and my caseload doubled. But even during those times, I still *wanted* things, you know? I still looked forward to having a day off, I still wanted to call my friends and vent, I still felt a deep sense of passion and righteous indignation about the systemic issues my clients were facing. It was exhaustion, but it wasn't... this. 

This complete absence of an internal life is entirely unprecedented for me. I’ve always been a very resilient person, the kind of person who could process a heavy week of trauma dumping from clients and bounce back by Monday because I had my coping mechanisms. So to suddenly find myself in this completely foreign landscape where I just don't have the capacity to care about anything... no, it's the very first time I've ever felt this profoundly disconnected from myself. And I think that lack of a frame of reference is what makes it so terrifying. I don't have a roadmap for this. I just keep waiting to wake up and feel like me again, to feel that little rush of empathy or curiosity, but the days just keep rolling by and it stays completely blank.
How long has this current period of feeling 'quiet' and disconnected lasted?

Well, that’s the thing, isn't it? Pinpointing the exact moment when the lights started going out. Because it didn't happen overnight, it wasn't like flipping a switch. It was more like... like a slow leak in a tire, where you don't realize how flat it is until you're struggling just to steer. But if I really sit down and trace it back, look at my calendar and my journal entries—or, well, the lack of journal entries—this whole change in how I'm thinking, working, and connecting with people... it's been going on for about eight months now. 

Yes, eight months. I can actually tie it to a very specific life event, which I suppose is helpful from a clinical standpoint. It started right around the time we took my older relative into our apartment. It was a whole transition, as you can imagine. We had to rearrange the spare room, figure out new routines, navigate the shifting family dynamics... and I initially thought the quietness, the withdrawal, was just a temporary reaction to that stress. You know, just my system being overloaded by the sudden lack of privacy and the added caretaking responsibilities on top of my already demanding job. I kept telling myself, "Once we get settled, once we find a rhythm, I'll get back to my yoga, I'll start feeling like myself again." But we did get settled, and the rhythm was found, and yet... the flatness just stayed. It didn't lift. And now here we are, eight months down the line, and I'm still just... blank. It's been eight months of just watching myself go through the motions from somewhere far away.
During these past eight months, have you experienced any periods where your symptoms were so severe that you were unable to function at work or perform your basic daily tasks?

Well, it’s… it’s a complicated question, isn't it? Because "functioning" is such a broad term, especially in our field. If you mean, am I getting out of bed, putting on professional clothes, and physically transporting myself to the clinic every day? Yes. I haven't taken any extended leaves of absence, I haven't been hospitalized, I haven't just stopped showing up. I am still physically present at work. I’m still sitting in my office. 

But… if you mean, am I functioning the way I *should* be functioning, the way I *used* to function? The answer is a very heavy, very resounding no. And that’s the part that really stings, because my professional identity has always been so central to who I am. 

I’ve always been the organized one, the one who could juggle a massive caseload and still have time to write meticulous, compelling grant proposals for the clinic. But over these last eight months, it’s like my executive functioning has just… evaporated. I’ll sit at my desk staring at a grant application that I know inside and out, and I just can’t make my brain organize the information. The words just swim on the page. I actually missed two major grant deadlines in the fall. Just completely let them slip by because I couldn’t muster the cognitive energy to finish them, which is so unlike me it’s almost laughable. 

And my clinical work… it hasn’t gone unnoticed. I thought I was hiding it well, just nodding and making the appropriate empathetic noises during sessions, but my supervisor—who is wonderful, we’ve worked together for over a decade—she noticed. She pulled me aside a few months ago for what she called a "check-in," but it was really an intervention. She’s been quietly, very gently, moving some of my more complex, high-needs clients off my roster. The ones who require intense crisis management or deep trauma processing… she’s been reassigning them to other clinicians. She framed it as "lightening my load during a difficult transition," but I know what it really means. She can see that I’m not functioning at my usual level. She can see that I don't have the emotional bandwidth to hold space for those clients right now. 

So, I’m still showing up, yes. I’m doing the bare minimum to keep my job. I handle the straightforward intakes, I do the routine follow-ups, I fill out the mandatory paperwork, eventually. But I am absolutely not the social worker I was a year ago. The quality of my work, my ability to actually effect change or handle complex cases… that’s been severely impaired. It’s like I’m a ghost haunting my own office, just going through the motions while everyone else quietly works around me.
Have you experienced any significant psychomotor agitation or retardation, such as feeling physically slowed down or unable to sit still, that others have commented on during these past eight months?

Agitation or... well, see, it’s not exactly that I’m pacing the floors or, you know, moving like I’m underwater. It’s not that classic physical restlessness or severe psychomotor retardation you might typically look for during an intake assessment. I'm not bouncing my leg off the floor or anything like that. But... there is something happening with my movements, and with my behavior, that people *have* definitely noticed. And honestly, it’s just mortifying. Because, like I said, I'm usually so composed, so in control of my presence in a room. 

What happens is... well, it’s these strange little actions. A few times recently, particularly in team meetings—we have these long Wednesday morning case reviews where we're all sitting around the big conference table—or, God forbid, even when I'm sitting one-on-one with clients... I’ve caught myself arranging my pens. But I don't mean just absentmindedly lining them up parallel to my notepad, which is a normal nervous habit. I mean I'll catch myself arranging them in these very specific, exact patterns. Like, meticulously placing them at these bizarre angles, over and over, completely lost in the physical act of doing it. 

And then there's the talking. Or the echoing, really. Someone will be speaking to me, and I will just... repeat a phrase they just said. Out loud. Right back to them, before I can even stop myself or realize what my mouth is doing. And I know how to do reflective listening, I'm a social worker, but this isn't that. It’s not a therapeutic technique. It's just this automatic, uncontrollable repetition of their words. 

And the looks I get... oh, the looks. People will just stop talking and look at me like... like I’ve completely stepped outside the room somehow. Like the lights are on but nobody's home. My supervisor gave me this exact look just last Tuesday when I repeated her sentence about a housing voucher, and the silence in the room was just deafening. I tried to play it off, to pretend I was just emphasizing her point, but you can't really hide that kind of bizarre behavior from a room full of trained mental health professionals. They know something is off. I know something is off. It's just so deeply embarrassing to be sitting there, realizing your hands or your mouth are doing these things without your permission, and not being able to explain to your colleagues why you're acting so... strangely.

Have you noticed any other physical symptoms, such as persistent headaches, vision changes, episodes of confusion, or any unexplained changes in your sense of taste or smell during these past eight months?

Physical symptoms like that... no. No, I really haven't. Which, as a clinician, I know exactly why you're asking. You're running down the list of differentials, right? Checking for organic causes, ruling out space-occupying lesions, neurological events, olfactory anomalies... I get it, I do the exact same thing during my own intakes when a client presents with a sudden behavioral or cognitive shift. It's just good clinical practice. But honestly, physically? In that specific sensory and neurological sense, I'm perfectly fine. 

You would think, given the immense amount of stress I was just talking about—with the apartment transition and the shifting family dynamics and the missed grant deadlines—that I’d at least be getting tension headaches. I used to get them all the time back in grad school, these terrible, tight bands of pain right across my forehead and at the base of my skull whenever I had a massive case study due. But lately? Nothing. My head doesn't hurt at all. It just feels... empty, like I was saying before. 

And my vision is completely stable. I actually just went to the optometrist back in, oh, I want to say October? Yes, October, because I had some FSA money I needed to use up before the end of the year, and my prescription hadn't changed even a quarter diopter. I'm still just wearing my standard reading glasses for the endless paperwork I'm barely getting through. 

As for confusion... I mean, I'm not disoriented to time or place. I know exactly where I am, I know what day it is, I know what I'm supposed to be doing. I'm not getting lost on my commute to the clinic or forgetting my clients' names or losing chunks of time. I just don't have the executive function or the emotional drive to do the work. 

And taste and smell... no, no changes there either. My morning coffee still tastes exactly like the same mediocre, slightly burnt roast it always has, and I can still smell the lavender essential oil my officemate diffuses every afternoon at two o'clock. So, no, none of those physical red flags. It’s almost frustrating, in a bizarre way, because if it were a sudden vision change or a blinding headache, there would be a clear, straightforward medical explanation for why I’m falling apart. You could just order an MRI and find a reason. But my body is functioning perfectly fine. It’s just... everything else that's unraveling.

During these past eight months, have you ever heard voices or seen things that others could not perceive, or have you had any thoughts that felt unusually intense or difficult to shake, even if you suspected they might not be entirely true?

Voices or seeing things... no. No, I haven't experienced any perceptual disturbances like that. The radio isn't talking to me, I'm not seeing shadows in the corners of my eyes. As a clinician, I know that's a key thing you need to rule in or out, but my reality testing on a purely sensory level is intact. 

But... the second part of your question. About thoughts that are intense or difficult to shake, even if I suspect they might not be true... that's where things get really, really uncomfortable for me to talk about. Because, logically, with my training, I know exactly how it sounds. I know it sounds unlikely, paranoid even. But I have become absolutely convinced—and I mean *convinced* in a way that I can't just logic myself out of—that I am being watched. Or, well, evaluated. Secretly monitored by the clinic.

It started with the staff emails. We get these weekly clinic updates, usually just administrative fluff about billing codes or reminders to empty the fridge on Fridays. But lately, I’ll read them, and there are these specific phrases... certain comments that feel entirely directed at me. Like, they'll mention "accountability in client documentation" or "maintaining professional presence," and I just *know* it’s a signal. It’s a message meant specifically to let me know they are tracking my decline. I’ll spend an hour just analyzing a two-paragraph email from the clinical director, parsing out the subtext, looking at the exact wording, because it feels so incredibly pointed. I'll read it over and over, trying to decode exactly what they're warning me about.

And it's not just the emails. It’s the physical space in the clinic, too. My office is near the end of the hall, right past the breakroom, so there's always foot traffic. But over the last few months, I’ve noticed the way people pause outside my door. They don't just walk by anymore. They stop. Just for a second or two, but it's enough. I can see their shadows under the door gap, or hear the squeak of their shoes stopping on the linoleum. And I know—I just feel it in my bones—that they are standing there listening. Trying to see if I'm actually working, or if I'm just sitting there staring at my desk. It’s this constant, suffocating feeling of being under surveillance by my own colleagues, the people I've worked with for years.

I actually brought this up to my supervisor. The same one who’s been reassigning my cases. I sat in her office a few weeks ago, and I was practically in tears, and I asked her point-blank if the board or the director had asked her to build a case against me. If there was a secret probationary file being put together. She was very empathetic, very validating—she used all the right active listening skills, assured me that absolutely no one was monitoring me, that the emails are just standard boilerplate, that people pausing in the hall are probably just checking their phones or catching their breath. 

And in the room, I nodded. I wanted to believe her. But the second I walked out? The feeling came right back. Her reassurance hasn't shaken it at all. If anything, a part of my brain just twisted it to think, "Well, of course she'd deny it if it were a covert evaluation." It's exhausting. I’m a mental health professional, I know what it means when a thought becomes that rigid, but I just can't make the feeling stop. I can't shake the conviction that they are all signaling to each other about me.
Have you noticed any difficulty with your memory, such as forgetting recent conversations or where you placed your belongings, that has developed alongside these other changes?

Memory? No, no, my memory is actually completely fine. It's sharp. I know exactly where my things are, always. You asked about belongings, and I can tell you my keys are always right in the little ceramic bowl by the front door—the one my niece painted for me a few years ago, it has these little uneven blue stars on it. I never lose my keys. My clinic ID badge is always clipped to my tote bag, the black leather one, right on the front left strap so I can just swipe it at the scanner without taking it off. I haven't lost my phone, I haven't misplaced my glasses... well, except when I push them up on top of my head and forget they're there, but everyone does that, right? That's just being forty-nine and tired, not a clinical memory deficit.

And as for conversations... no, I remember everything. Honestly, sometimes I wish I could forget. Like I was saying about that meeting with my supervisor—I can tell you exactly what she said, word for word. I remember she was wearing this mustard yellow cardigan, and she leaned forward, resting her elbows on her desk, and said, "I want to make sure you feel supported here." I remember the exact intonation of her voice, the way she paused before the word 'supported.' My working memory, my short-term recall, it's all perfectly intact. If you gave me three words to remember right now, you know, like we do in a standard cognitive screen, I could repeat them back to you in five minutes, no problem. Apple, penny, table, whatever it is. 

So it's definitely not a cognitive decline in that sense. My brain holds onto the information perfectly well. In fact, it holds onto it almost too well, because I'm constantly replaying those conversations, analyzing them, like I mentioned with the emails. I remember every single word of those staff emails. I can practically quote the clinical director's last update about the new Medicaid billing codes. So, no, my memory isn't the problem at all. The problem is... well, it's what my brain is doing with the information once it's in there, you know? It's the way I'm interpreting the things I remember so clearly. Because I remember the footsteps outside my door, too. I remember exactly how long they pause. I remember the exact dates I started noticing the shadows under the door. So the memory is there, it's just... it's everything else that's making it so hard to function.

Do you feel that you are being monitored or targeted only by your colleagues at the clinic, or do you have the same sense that you are being watched or evaluated when you are at home or in other settings?

At home? No... no, honestly, it’s really just at the clinic. When I’m at home, in my apartment, I actually feel safe. I mean, I lock the deadbolt, I put my keys in that little star bowl I told you about, and I know I’m alone. I’m not, you know, checking the smoke detectors for hidden cameras or thinking the neighbors are listening to me through the drywall or anything like that. It’s nothing like that. It is entirely, one hundred percent localized to my workplace. 

Which is why, like I was saying just a minute ago—and I know I’m circling back to this, but it’s just taking up so much space in my head right now, it's so hard to move past it—I know it sounds so unlikely. I really do. If one of my own clients sat on my couch and said this, I’d be gently exploring their reality testing. But I have just become so deeply, utterly convinced that those certain comments in the staff emails, and even the specific way people are pausing outside my office... I know they are meant to signal that I’m being watched or evaluated. It’s not just a passing professional anxiety; it’s a concrete knowing. 

And it’s incredibly frustrating because, like I mentioned, the reassurance from my supervisor hasn’t really shaken that feeling at all. I can sit in my living room on a Saturday morning, drinking my chamomile tea, and logically tell myself, 'She said you aren't being investigated. The emails are just emails.' I can try to do the cognitive reframing, use all the CBT tools I teach my clients. But the second Monday morning rolls around and I swipe my leather tote bag at the clinic entrance? It’s like a physical weight drops on my chest. I’ll see the receptionist glance up from her computer, or I’ll hear a pair of heels stop clicking right outside my door, and that absolute certainty just floods right back in. 

So, no, it doesn’t follow me to the grocery store or into my living room. But because my career is my entire life, especially now... having my workplace feel like this giant, coordinated surveillance operation against me... it’s completely paralyzing. I just can't turn it off once I'm in that building.

patient.answer:
You know, I’ve been asking myself that exact same question for weeks now. Because, naturally, given my training, I try to psychoanalyze myself—which is a terrible habit, I know, we make the worst patients. But I’ve really been digging through my own history, trying to find some sort of precedent for this, looking for a pattern. And... no. I really haven't. 

I mean, sure, I’ve had periods of professional burnout. When I was finishing my master's degree in my twenties, for instance, I was working full-time while doing my clinical field placements, and I was just absolutely bone-tired. I’d come home and just collapse on the couch. Or even a few years ago, when our clinic was understaffed and my caseload doubled. But even during those times, I still *wanted* things, you know? I still looked forward to having a day off, I still wanted to call my friends and vent, I still felt a deep sense of passion and righteous indignation about the systemic issues my clients were facing. It was exhaustion, but it wasn't... this. 

This complete absence of an internal life is entirely unprecedented for me. I’ve always been a very resilient person, the kind of person who could process a heavy week of trauma dumping from clients and bounce back by Monday because I had my coping mechanisms. So to suddenly find myself in this completely foreign landscape where I just don't have the capacity to care about anything... no, it's the very first time I've ever felt this profoundly disconnected from myself. And I think that lack of a frame of reference is what makes it so terrifying. I don't have a roadmap for this. I just keep waiting to wake up and feel like me again, to feel that little rush of empathy or curiosity, but the days just keep rolling by and it stays completely blank.

patient.answer:
Well, that’s the thing, isn't it? Pinpointing the exact moment when the lights started going out. Because it didn't happen overnight, it wasn't like flipping a switch. It was more like... like a slow leak in a tire, where you don't realize how flat it is until you're struggling just to steer. But if I really sit down and trace it back, look at my calendar and my journal entries—or, well, the lack of journal entries—this whole change in how I'm thinking, working, and connecting with people... it's been going on for about eight months now. 

Yes, eight months. I can actually tie it to a very specific life event, which I suppose is helpful from a clinical standpoint. It started right around the time we took my older relative into our apartment. It was a whole transition, as you can imagine. We had to rearrange the spare room, figure out new routines, navigate the shifting family dynamics... and I initially thought the quietness, the withdrawal, was just a temporary reaction to that stress. You know, just my system being overloaded by the sudden lack of privacy and the added caretaking responsibilities on top of my already demanding job. I kept telling myself, "Once we get settled, once we find a rhythm, I'll get back to my yoga, I'll start feeling like myself again." But we did get settled, and the rhythm was found, and yet... the flatness just stayed. It didn't lift. And now here we are, eight months down the line, and I'm still just... blank. It's been eight months of just watching myself go through the motions from somewhere far away.

inference.note: Given the duration of eight months and the severity of the symptoms (anhedonia, emotional detachment, loss of interest), I am shifting focus toward recurrent depressive disorder (F33.x) rather than single episode, as the patient describes this as a profound departure from her baseline personality and resilience. F34.1 remains a consideration due to the chronic nature, but the intensity of the current impairment points more toward a major depressive episode.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between recurrent depression (F33.x) and persistent depressive disorder (F34.1) by assessing for the presence of severe depressive episodes that meet full criteria.
doctor.question: During these past eight months, have you experienced any periods where your symptoms were so severe that you were unable to function at work or perform your basic daily tasks?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up to work, but I’ve missed grant deadlines and my supervisor has quietly moved some of my more demanding clients to other clinicians because I’m not functioning at my usual level.
target_item.reason: The doctor is explicitly asking about my ability to function at work and perform daily tasks, which directly corresponds to the Functional Impairment profile.

patient.answer:
Well, it’s… it’s a complicated question, isn't it? Because "functioning" is such a broad term, especially in our field. If you mean, am I getting out of bed, putting on professional clothes, and physically transporting myself to the clinic every day? Yes. I haven't taken any extended leaves of absence, I haven't been hospitalized, I haven't just stopped showing up. I am still physically present at work. I’m still sitting in my office. 

But… if you mean, am I functioning the way I *should* be functioning, the way I *used* to function? The answer is a very heavy, very resounding no. And that’s the part that really stings, because my professional identity has always been so central to who I am. 

I’ve always been the organized one, the one who could juggle a massive caseload and still have time to write meticulous, compelling grant proposals for the clinic. But over these last eight months, it’s like my executive functioning has just… evaporated. I’ll sit at my desk staring at a grant application that I know inside and out, and I just can’t make my brain organize the information. The words just swim on the page. I actually missed two major grant deadlines in the fall. Just completely let them slip by because I couldn’t muster the cognitive energy to finish them, which is so unlike me it’s almost laughable. 

And my clinical work… it hasn’t gone unnoticed. I thought I was hiding it well, just nodding and making the appropriate empathetic noises during sessions, but my supervisor—who is wonderful, we’ve worked together for over a decade—she noticed. She pulled me aside a few months ago for what she called a "check-in," but it was really an intervention. She’s been quietly, very gently, moving some of my more complex, high-needs clients off my roster. The ones who require intense crisis management or deep trauma processing… she’s been reassigning them to other clinicians. She framed it as "lightening my load during a difficult transition," but I know what it really means. She can see that I’m not functioning at my usual level. She can see that I don't have the emotional bandwidth to hold space for those clients right now. 

So, I’m still showing up, yes. I’m doing the bare minimum to keep my job. I handle the straightforward intakes, I do the routine follow-ups, I fill out the mandatory paperwork, eventually. But I am absolutely not the social worker I was a year ago. The quality of my work, my ability to actually effect change or handle complex cases… that’s been severely impaired. It’s like I’m a ghost haunting my own office, just going through the motions while everyone else quietly works around me.

inference.note: Ruled out F34.1 (Persistent Depressive Disorder) because the patient describes a discrete, severe episode of 8 months that represents a clear departure from her baseline functioning, rather than a chronic, low-grade depression of at least 2 years.

doctor.intent: To determine the severity and nature of the patient's impairment to differentiate between moderate (F33.1) and severe (F33.2) depression.
doctor.question: Have you experienced any significant psychomotor agitation or retardation, such as feeling physically slowed down or unable to sit still, that others have commented on during these past eight months?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: A few times in team meetings or even with clients, I’ve caught myself arranging pens in these exact patterns or repeating a phrase someone just said before I can stop myself, and people look at me like I’ve stepped outside the room somehow.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in motor control or behavior, such as psychomotor agitation or retardation. This corresponds to the patient's disorganized and abnormal behavior, specifically the stereotyped movements and echolalia.

patient.answer:
Agitation or... well, see, it’s not exactly that I’m pacing the floors or, you know, moving like I’m underwater. It’s not that classic physical restlessness or severe psychomotor retardation you might typically look for during an intake assessment. I'm not bouncing my leg off the floor or anything like that. But... there is something happening with my movements, and with my behavior, that people *have* definitely noticed. And honestly, it’s just mortifying. Because, like I said, I'm usually so composed, so in control of my presence in a room. 

What happens is... well, it’s these strange little actions. A few times recently, particularly in team meetings—we have these long Wednesday morning case reviews where we're all sitting around the big conference table—or, God forbid, even when I'm sitting one-on-one with clients... I’ve caught myself arranging my pens. But I don't mean just absentmindedly lining them up parallel to my notepad, which is a normal nervous habit. I mean I'll catch myself arranging them in these very specific, exact patterns. Like, meticulously placing them at these bizarre angles, over and over, completely lost in the physical act of doing it. 

And then there's the talking. Or the echoing, really. Someone will be speaking to me, and I will just... repeat a phrase they just said. Out loud. Right back to them, before I can even stop myself or realize what my mouth is doing. And I know how to do reflective listening, I'm a social worker, but this isn't that. It’s not a therapeutic technique. It's just this automatic, uncontrollable repetition of their words. 

And the looks I get... oh, the looks. People will just stop talking and look at me like... like I’ve completely stepped outside the room somehow. Like the lights are on but nobody's home. My supervisor gave me this exact look just last Tuesday when I repeated her sentence about a housing voucher, and the silence in the room was just deafening. I tried to play it off, to pretend I was just emphasizing her point, but you can't really hide that kind of bizarre behavior from a room full of trained mental health professionals. They know something is off. I know something is off. It's just so deeply embarrassing to be sitting there, realizing your hands or your mouth are doing these things without your permission, and not being able to explain to your colleagues why you're acting so... strangely.

inference.note: The patient's report of echolalia and repetitive, ritualistic motor behaviors (stereotypies) in a professional setting is highly atypical for pure Major Depressive Disorder and raises the possibility of an underlying organic or neurological process (F06.3) contributing to the clinical presentation.

doctor.intent: To determine if there is an underlying organic or neurological cause for the patient's sudden onset of bizarre, repetitive behaviors (echolalia and stereotypic movements) which would point toward F06.3 (Mood disorder due to a known physiological condition) rather than a primary psychiatric disorder.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any other physical symptoms, such as persistent headaches, vision changes, episodes of confusion, or any unexplained changes in your sense of taste or smell during these past eight months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical or neurological symptoms such as headaches, vision changes, confusion, or changes in taste/smell, which are not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Physical symptoms like that... no. No, I really haven't. Which, as a clinician, I know exactly why you're asking. You're running down the list of differentials, right? Checking for organic causes, ruling out space-occupying lesions, neurological events, olfactory anomalies... I get it, I do the exact same thing during my own intakes when a client presents with a sudden behavioral or cognitive shift. It's just good clinical practice. But honestly, physically? In that specific sensory and neurological sense, I'm perfectly fine. 

You would think, given the immense amount of stress I was just talking about—with the apartment transition and the shifting family dynamics and the missed grant deadlines—that I’d at least be getting tension headaches. I used to get them all the time back in grad school, these terrible, tight bands of pain right across my forehead and at the base of my skull whenever I had a massive case study due. But lately? Nothing. My head doesn't hurt at all. It just feels... empty, like I was saying before. 

And my vision is completely stable. I actually just went to the optometrist back in, oh, I want to say October? Yes, October, because I had some FSA money I needed to use up before the end of the year, and my prescription hadn't changed even a quarter diopter. I'm still just wearing my standard reading glasses for the endless paperwork I'm barely getting through. 

As for confusion... I mean, I'm not disoriented to time or place. I know exactly where I am, I know what day it is, I know what I'm supposed to be doing. I'm not getting lost on my commute to the clinic or forgetting my clients' names or losing chunks of time. I just don't have the executive function or the emotional drive to do the work. 

And taste and smell... no, no changes there either. My morning coffee still tastes exactly like the same mediocre, slightly burnt roast it always has, and I can still smell the lavender essential oil my officemate diffuses every afternoon at two o'clock. So, no, none of those physical red flags. It’s almost frustrating, in a bizarre way, because if it were a sudden vision change or a blinding headache, there would be a clear, straightforward medical explanation for why I’m falling apart. You could just order an MRI and find a reason. But my body is functioning perfectly fine. It’s just... everything else that's unraveling.

inference.note: The patient's report of echolalia and stereotyped, repetitive motor behaviors (arranging pens) in a professional setting, combined with an 8-month duration and the absence of clear primary mood symptoms, necessitates the inclusion of F06.8 (Other specified mental disorders due to known physiological condition) to account for potential underlying neurological or organic pathology that mimics a mood disorder.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between a primary mood disorder and a secondary condition by checking for the presence of mood-congruent or mood-incongruent delusions or hallucinations.
doctor.question: During these past eight months, have you ever heard voices or seen things that others could not perceive, or have you had any thoughts that felt unusually intense or difficult to shake, even if you suspected they might not be entirely true?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds unlikely, but I’ve become convinced that certain comments in staff emails and even the way people pause outside my office are meant to signal that I’m being watched or evaluated, and reassurance from my supervisor hasn’t really shaken that feeling.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hallucinations and intense, hard-to-shake beliefs or thoughts, which maps directly to my symptoms of delusions.

patient.answer:
Voices or seeing things... no. No, I haven't experienced any perceptual disturbances like that. The radio isn't talking to me, I'm not seeing shadows in the corners of my eyes. As a clinician, I know that's a key thing you need to rule in or out, but my reality testing on a purely sensory level is intact. 

But... the second part of your question. About thoughts that are intense or difficult to shake, even if I suspect they might not be true... that's where things get really, really uncomfortable for me to talk about. Because, logically, with my training, I know exactly how it sounds. I know it sounds unlikely, paranoid even. But I have become absolutely convinced—and I mean *convinced* in a way that I can't just logic myself out of—that I am being watched. Or, well, evaluated. Secretly monitored by the clinic.

It started with the staff emails. We get these weekly clinic updates, usually just administrative fluff about billing codes or reminders to empty the fridge on Fridays. But lately, I’ll read them, and there are these specific phrases... certain comments that feel entirely directed at me. Like, they'll mention "accountability in client documentation" or "maintaining professional presence," and I just *know* it’s a signal. It’s a message meant specifically to let me know they are tracking my decline. I’ll spend an hour just analyzing a two-paragraph email from the clinical director, parsing out the subtext, looking at the exact wording, because it feels so incredibly pointed. I'll read it over and over, trying to decode exactly what they're warning me about.

And it's not just the emails. It’s the physical space in the clinic, too. My office is near the end of the hall, right past the breakroom, so there's always foot traffic. But over the last few months, I’ve noticed the way people pause outside my door. They don't just walk by anymore. They stop. Just for a second or two, but it's enough. I can see their shadows under the door gap, or hear the squeak of their shoes stopping on the linoleum. And I know—I just feel it in my bones—that they are standing there listening. Trying to see if I'm actually working, or if I'm just sitting there staring at my desk. It’s this constant, suffocating feeling of being under surveillance by my own colleagues, the people I've worked with for years.

I actually brought this up to my supervisor. The same one who’s been reassigning my cases. I sat in her office a few weeks ago, and I was practically in tears, and I asked her point-blank if the board or the director had asked her to build a case against me. If there was a secret probationary file being put together. She was very empathetic, very validating—she used all the right active listening skills, assured me that absolutely no one was monitoring me, that the emails are just standard boilerplate, that people pausing in the hall are probably just checking their phones or catching their breath. 

And in the room, I nodded. I wanted to believe her. But the second I walked out? The feeling came right back. Her reassurance hasn't shaken it at all. If anything, a part of my brain just twisted it to think, "Well, of course she'd deny it if it were a covert evaluation." It's exhausting. I’m a mental health professional, I know what it means when a thought becomes that rigid, but I just can't make the feeling stop. I can't shake the conviction that they are all signaling to each other about me.

inference.note: The patient's clinical presentation, specifically the development of fixed, persecutory delusions (ideas of reference and surveillance) in the absence of primary sensory hallucinations or cognitive impairment, shifts the focus from purely mood-based disorders to a psychotic process, likely secondary or primary.

doctor.intent: Distinguish between primary psychosis (F20.89) or delusional disorder (F22) versus a secondary psychiatric presentation due to a neurological or medical condition (F06.2) by assessing the presence of cognitive impairment beyond just executive dysfunction.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any difficulty with your memory, such as forgetting recent conversations or where you placed your belongings, that has developed alongside these other changes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about memory issues or cognitive impairment, which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Memory? No, no, my memory is actually completely fine. It's sharp. I know exactly where my things are, always. You asked about belongings, and I can tell you my keys are always right in the little ceramic bowl by the front door—the one my niece painted for me a few years ago, it has these little uneven blue stars on it. I never lose my keys. My clinic ID badge is always clipped to my tote bag, the black leather one, right on the front left strap so I can just swipe it at the scanner without taking it off. I haven't lost my phone, I haven't misplaced my glasses... well, except when I push them up on top of my head and forget they're there, but everyone does that, right? That's just being forty-nine and tired, not a clinical memory deficit.

And as for conversations... no, I remember everything. Honestly, sometimes I wish I could forget. Like I was saying about that meeting with my supervisor—I can tell you exactly what she said, word for word. I remember she was wearing this mustard yellow cardigan, and she leaned forward, resting her elbows on her desk, and said, "I want to make sure you feel supported here." I remember the exact intonation of her voice, the way she paused before the word 'supported.' My working memory, my short-term recall, it's all perfectly intact. If you gave me three words to remember right now, you know, like we do in a standard cognitive screen, I could repeat them back to you in five minutes, no problem. Apple, penny, table, whatever it is. 

So it's definitely not a cognitive decline in that sense. My brain holds onto the information perfectly well. In fact, it holds onto it almost too well, because I'm constantly replaying those conversations, analyzing them, like I mentioned with the emails. I remember every single word of those staff emails. I can practically quote the clinical director's last update about the new Medicaid billing codes. So, no, my memory isn't the problem at all. The problem is... well, it's what my brain is doing with the information once it's in there, you know? It's the way I'm interpreting the things I remember so clearly. Because I remember the footsteps outside my door, too. I remember exactly how long they pause. I remember the exact dates I started noticing the shadows under the door. So the memory is there, it's just... it's everything else that's making it so hard to function.

inference.note: Ruled out F06.2 due to the patient's explicit denial of memory impairment, confusion, or other cognitive deficits, and the absence of any neurological or sensory-perceptual red flags that would suggest an organic cause.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's beliefs about being monitored are limited to the workplace or if they extend to other areas of life to differentiate between a circumscribed delusional system (F22) and broader schizophrenia spectrum features (F20.89).
doctor.question: Do you feel that you are being monitored or targeted only by your colleagues at the clinic, or do you have the same sense that you are being watched or evaluated when you are at home or in other settings?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds unlikely, but I’ve become convinced that certain comments in staff emails and even the way people pause outside my office are meant to signal that I’m being watched or evaluated, and reassurance from my supervisor hasn’t really shaken that feeling.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking a follow-up question about the patient's paranoid beliefs of being monitored or evaluated, which falls under delusions.

patient.answer:
At home? No... no, honestly, it’s really just at the clinic. When I’m at home, in my apartment, I actually feel safe. I mean, I lock the deadbolt, I put my keys in that little star bowl I told you about, and I know I’m alone. I’m not, you know, checking the smoke detectors for hidden cameras or thinking the neighbors are listening to me through the drywall or anything like that. It’s nothing like that. It is entirely, one hundred percent localized to my workplace. 

Which is why, like I was saying just a minute ago—and I know I’m circling back to this, but it’s just taking up so much space in my head right now, it's so hard to move past it—I know it sounds so unlikely. I really do. If one of my own clients sat on my couch and said this, I’d be gently exploring their reality testing. But I have just become so deeply, utterly convinced that those certain comments in the staff emails, and even the specific way people are pausing outside my office... I know they are meant to signal that I’m being watched or evaluated. It’s not just a passing professional anxiety; it’s a concrete knowing. 

And it’s incredibly frustrating because, like I mentioned, the reassurance from my supervisor hasn’t really shaken that feeling at all. I can sit in my living room on a Saturday morning, drinking my chamomile tea, and logically tell myself, 'She said you aren't being investigated. The emails are just emails.' I can try to do the cognitive reframing, use all the CBT tools I teach my clients. But the second Monday morning rolls around and I swipe my leather tote bag at the clinic entrance? It’s like a physical weight drops on my chest. I’ll see the receptionist glance up from her computer, or I’ll hear a pair of heels stop clicking right outside my door, and that absolute certainty just floods right back in. 

So, no, it doesn’t follow me to the grocery store or into my living room. But because my career is my entire life, especially now... having my workplace feel like this giant, coordinated surveillance operation against me... it’s completely paralyzing. I just can't turn it off once I'm in that building.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms are localized to a specific, plausible theme (workplace surveillance/evaluation) and lack the broader, disorganized, or pervasive psychotic features (such as cognitive decline, hallucinations, or generalized paranoia) that would characterize F20.89. The duration of 8 months and the specific nature of the delusional system point more strongly toward a delusional disorder.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and identify the patient's primary reason for seeking psychiatric consultation.
opening_question.question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a persistent, systematized delusional belief regarding workplace surveillance (persecutory themes localized to the clinic) without other prominent psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, disorganized speech, or catatonic behavior. The delusion has lasted for 8 months, causing significant functional impairment, while cognitive function and other reality testing remain largely intact.
